source.text: Ἄκουε, φησίν, περὶ τῶν τριῶν μορφῶν ὧν ἐπιζητεῖς. 2. τῇ μὲν πρώτῃ ὁράσει διατί πρεσβυτέρα ὤφθη σοι καὶ ἐπὶ καθέδραν καθημένη; ὅτι τὸ πνεῦμα ὑμῶν πρεσβύτερον καὶ ἤδη μεμαρασμένον καὶ μὴ ἔχον δύναμιν ἀπὸ τῶν μαλακιῶν ὑμῶν καὶ διψυχιῶν. 3. ὥσπερ γὰρ οἱ πρεσβύτεροι, μηκέτι ἔχοντες ἐλπίδα τοῦ ἀνανεῶσαι, οὐδὲν ἄλλο προσδοκῶσιν εἰ μὴ τὴν κοίμησιν αὐτῶν, οὕτω καὶ ὑμεῖς μαλακισθέντες ἀπὸ τῶν βιωτικῶν πραγμάτων παρεδώκατε ἑαυτοὺς εἰς τὰς ἀκηδίας, καὶ οὐκ ἐπερίψατε ἑαυτῶν τὰς μερίμνας ἐπὶ τὸν Κύριον· ἀλλὰ ἐθραύσθη ὑμῶν ἡ διάνοια, καὶ ἐπαλαιώθητε ταῖς λύπαις ὑμῶν. 4. Διατί οὖν ἐν καθέδρᾳ ἐκάθητο, ἤθελον γνῶναι, κύριε. Ὅτι πᾶς ἀσθενὴς εἰς καθέδραν καθέζεται διὰ τὴν ἀσθένειαν αὐτοῦ, ἵνα συνκρατηθῇ ἡ ἀσθένεια τοῦ σώματος αὐτοῦ. ἔχεις τὸν τύπον τῆς πρώτης ὁράσεως.
source.label: Vision 3, section xi

translation.text:
“Listen,” he says[1], “about the three forms you are inquiring about. In the first vision, why did she appear to you as an old woman and seated on a chair? Because your spirit is old and already withered and has no strength because of your softness and your double‑mindedness. For just as the aged, no longer having hope of being renewed, expect nothing else but their sleep,[1] so also you, having been softened by the affairs of life, have handed yourselves over to negligence,[2] and you did not cast your anxieties upon the Lord;[4] instead your mind has been shattered, and you have grown old in your sorrows.”

“Why then was she seated in a chair? I would like to know, sir.”[3] “Because every weak person sits in a chair because of his weakness, in order that the weakness of his body may be steadied[a][5][4][3][2]. You have the pattern of the first vision.”[5]

footnotes.text: “Sleep” is a common early Christian euphemism for death.
The Greek term is ἀκηδία (“acedia”), meaning neglect, lack of care, or listless indifference.
Vocative κύριε here is a respectful “sir,” addressed to the interpreter; distinct from “the Lord” (God) in the previous clause.
Compare 1 Peter 5:7, which uses the same verb (“cast”) for placing anxieties upon the Lord.
“Pattern” translates τύπος, which can also mean “type,” “figure,” or “model”; here it denotes the explanation corresponding to the first vision.
Or '“Why then was she seated in a chair? I wanted to know, sir.”'.

lexical_decisions.rationale: μορφή refers to external form or appearance; “forms” preserves the visionary imagery without over‑interpreting.
Context is interpretive inquiry into symbols, so “are inquiring about” fits better than simple “seek.”
ὅρασις in apocalyptic contexts is best rendered “vision.”
Concrete image of a woman advanced in years; avoids confusion with ecclesial office implied by “elder.”
Concrete furniture term; “chair” aligns with the action of sitting and the weakness image.
Hermas uses “spirit” for the human inner disposition; context contrasts vigor vs. withering. Not the Holy Spirit.
The perfect participle conveys a settled state; “withered” captures the image vividly.
Physical and moral vigor is in view; “strength” is idiomatic.
μαλακία denotes moral softness/laxity; rendered as a mass noun in English to avoid awkward plural.
Established ethical term in early Christian literature; keeps the concrete metaphor of being “two‑souled.”
Here the reference is to age, not to church elders; “the aged” avoids ecclesial confusion.
General renewal, not a technical theological term; “be renewed” is concise.
Maintains the euphemism common in early Christian diction; clarified by footnote.
Neutral phrase that captures mundane, this‑worldly concerns without moralizing the term itself.
Carries the causal link to the earlier “softness”; avoids pejorative connotations of “effeminate” in modern English.
Mass‑noun rendering fits English idiom; footnote notes the traditional term “acedia.”
μερίμνα often denotes anxious concern; “anxieties” balances concreteness and readability.
Preserves the vivid act of off‑loading cares onto the Lord; echoes but does not import NT diction beyond the Greek itself.
Reference is to God; default rendering in Cartha is “Lord.”
The inner faculty of thought/resolve; “mind” fits the contrast with being shattered.
θραύω is a strong verb for breaking; “shattered” conveys the severity.
Idiomatic English that preserves metaphor of aging through sorrow.
Plural concrete burdens; “sorrows” preserves the affective weight.
Physical frailty is the image; “weak/weakness” is straightforward.
The aim is to stabilize bodily weakness; “be steadied” is vivid and idiomatic.
Here denotes the corresponding explanation/figure to the vision; “pattern” is clear, with footnote noting alternatives.
Polite address to the visionary interpreter, distinguished from “the Lord” (God) in the same unit.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Human inner disposition (“your spirit”), not the Holy Spirit
theological_decisions.rationale: Context contrasts vigor and withering due to moral failings; this is about the audience’s interior state, not a claim about the Holy Spirit.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Translate vocative κύριε to the messenger as “sir,” but ὁ Κύριος as “the Lord” for God
theological_decisions.rationale: The same lemma appears with different referents; maintaining a distinction avoids blurring divine title with polite address.
theological_decisions.doctrine_reference: Translation philosophy: Titles translated; names transliterated.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Render κοίμησις as “sleep,” preserving the euphemism for death
theological_decisions.rationale: Early Christian idiom often speaks of death as sleep; preserving it maintains the texture and allows readers to note the metaphor.
theological_decisions.doctrine_reference: Preserve theological tension and imagery; avoid flattening.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Render πρεσβύτεροι here as “the aged,” not “elders” (office)
theological_decisions.rationale: The comparison is with human aging and loss of vigor; not with church governance.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Translate as “negligence,” noting the traditional term “acedia” in a footnote
theological_decisions.rationale: “Negligence” communicates the lack of care/concern in context; footnote preserves historical term.
theological_decisions.doctrine_reference: Readable modern English without flattening theological weight.

review_passes.summary: The draft is generally excellent, but has a few minor issues: `τῇ μὲν πρώτῃ ὁράσει` is better rendered 'In the first vision', `ὤφθη` is the standard term for 'appeared' rather than 'was shown', and `τοῦ ἀνανεῶσαι` is an active infinitive ('of renewal'). Additionally, the draft placed 'I wanted to know, sir' outside the quotation marks, but the vocative `κύριε` shows it is spoken directly to the young man.
issues_found: Mistranslation: 'As to the first vision' loosely translates the dative of time/sphere `τῇ μὲν πρώτῃ ὁράσει`; 'In the first vision' is more direct.
Lexical choice: 'was she shown to you' translates `ὤφθη σοι`, but `ὤφθη` is the standard aorist for visionary appearances ('did she appear to you').
Grammar: 'of being renewed' translates `τοῦ ἀνανεῶσαι`, which is an active infinitive ('of renewal' or 'of renewing').
Punctuation/Grammar: The draft places 'I wanted to know, sir' outside the quotation marks, but the vocative `κύριε` indicates it is addressed to the young man and belongs inside the dialogue.

base_translation.text: “Listen,” he says, “about the three forms you are inquiring about. In the first vision, why did she appear to you as an old woman and seated on a chair? Because your spirit is old and already withered and has no strength because of your weaknesses and your double‑mindedness. For just as the aged, no longer having hope of being renewed, expect nothing else but their sleep, so also you, having been weakened by the affairs of life, have handed yourselves over to negligence, and you did not cast your anxieties upon the Lord; instead your mind has been shattered, and you have grown old in your sorrows.”

translation.text: “Listen,” he says, “and I will explain the three forms you asked about. Why did she appear in the first vision as an old woman sitting in a chair? Because your spirit had grown old and withered. Your weaknesses and divided mind had left it without strength. Old people who no longer hope to be renewed expect nothing but sleep. In the same way, the affairs of life have weakened you all. You have given yourselves over to neglect and have not cast your anxieties upon the Lord. Instead, your minds have been shattered, and you have grown old in your sorrows.”

spob_revision_history.previous_text: “Listen,” he says, “and I will explain the three forms you asked about. Why did she appear in the first vision as an old woman sitting in a chair? It was because your spirit had grown old and withered. Your weaknesses and divided loyalty had left it without strength. Old people who no longer hope to regain their strength expect nothing but sleep. In the same way, the troubles of life have weakened you all. You have given yourselves over to neglect and have not cast your anxieties upon the Lord. Instead, your minds have been shattered, and sorrow has made you old.”
spob_revision_history.review_summary: The draft substantially improves readability through direct questions, shorter clauses, and explicit causal connections, while correctly retaining the unresolved image of “sleep” and the singular-to-plural shift. Revision is needed in two places: “divided loyalty” over-specifies double-mindedness, and “regain their strength” contracts the stated hope of renewal. The recommended wording preserves the broader source sense while remaining accessible.
